newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia begins debate on 1997/98 migrant numbers.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia begins debate on 1997/98 migrant numbers.

text.p: The Australian government on Monday called for public debate to help set the size and make-up of its immigration programme, which critics say is too high and allows too many Asians into the country.
Immigration Minister Philip Ruddock, beginning annual community consultations to set a limit for migrant numbers in the year to June 30, 1998, called for an open and objective community debate.

"Many recent statements criticising migrants and migration have been, at best, misconceived or ill-informed and do nothing to enhance Australia's reputation as a tolerant and cohesive society," Ruddock said at a press conference.
"There has been a great deal of comment that has focussed on a very narrow range of issues, particularly issues of race. A lot of comments have been based on narrow perceptions," he said.
Australia has been wracked by a row over Asian immigration since independent parliamentarian Pauline Hanson last year said Australia was in danger of being swamped by Asians.

Opinion polls showed most Australians supported her views, but Prime Minister John Howard and other political leaders have rejected her comments and pledged Australia would not discriminate against immigrants on the basis of race.
The controversy prompted warnings from Asian countries that Australia's regional standing and lucrative trade with its booming neighbours were being jeopardised.
Ruddock said immigration had helped shape Australia and made it a culturally diverse country.
"The government believes we have matured as a nation as a result of that diversity," he said.
Ruddock released a government study on the impact of immigration, which he said debunked the myths and misperceptions of the anti-immigration debate.
The study found Asian-born Australians were on average more skilled than Australians and made up less than 4.5 percent of Australia's 18 million population.
Although Asians now account for about 40 percent of new migrants, the number of Asian-born migrants would only rise to 7.5 percent of the population in 30 years on current trends.
"They do not constitute figures that ought to be of concern to any Australian," said Ruddock, reaffirming the government's commitment to a non-discriminatory immigration policy.

"One issue that is not negotiable in any debate is that immigration to Australia must be based upon the principle of non-discrimination in terms of race, religion, colour and ethnic background," he said.
The government would maintain tight security and health checks and a high priority on professional and English language skills, he added.

Australia's conservative government cut migrant numbers soon after it ousted the ruling Labor party in March 1996, setting a limit of 74,000 migrants in 1996/97, compared with the 82,500 set by Labor in 1995/96. The figures do not include about 13,000 arrivals under humanitarian and refugee programmes.
Ruddock will meet about 2,000 individuals and community groups, including ethnic organisations and religious leaders, before announcing the migrant limit by July.
